effect_estimate.comment: Note on PDF font encoding: in the extracted PDF text of Table 4 (p. 11), minus signs are omitted by font glyph encoding, but the negative signs for 2001 baseline coverage (-0.173, SE = 0.011/0.012, p < 0.01), intergovernmental aid (-0.034, SE = 0.015, p < 0.05), small cities (-5.122) and small towns (-5.432), and municipalities (-4.062) and town panchayats (-4.034) are explicitly confirmed in the Results prose on PDF pp. 10-12.
effect_estimate.value: Across 3,547 Indian cities (2001-2011), mean household tap-water coverage growth was +5.08 percentage points (SD = 12.64), with 68% of cities recording increases. Descriptively (Table 3), coverage grew by +6.86 percentage points in municipal corporations (52.22% to 59.08%), +5.02 in municipalities (43.93% to 48.95%), and +5.01 in town panchayats and others (30.31% to 35.34%); by size, +7.22 in metropolitan cities, +5.73 in medium cities, +4.63 in small cities, and +5.11 in small towns. In multilevel linear regressions (Table 4, N = 3,547 cities in 21 states), relative to metropolitan cities (Model 1), small cities (-5.122 percentage points, SE = 2.011, p < 0.05) and small towns (-5.432 percentage points, SE = 2.209, p < 0.05) had significantly lower coverage growth (medium cities: -2.238, SE = 2.504, NS). Relative to municipal corporations (Model 2), lower-tier local governments had significantly lower coverage growth: municipalities (-4.062 percentage points, SE = 1.254, p < 0.01) and town panchayats and others (-4.034 percentage points, SE = 1.540, p < 0.01). Per-capita NURM/UIDSSMT intergovernmental aid was negatively associated with coverage growth (-0.034 percentage points per rupee per 1,000 persons, SE = 0.015, p < 0.05 in both models), state income (2004 NSDP per capita) was positively associated (+0.001 percentage points per rupee, i.e., +1.0 percentage point per 1,000 rupees, SE = 0.000, p < 0.01), and the state fiscal decentralization index was not statistically significant (coefficient magnitude 2.011, SE = 3.949 in Model 1; 2.016, SE = 3.936 in Model 2).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 6, Table 1; PDF p. 8 and p. 10, Table 3; PDF pp. 10-12, Model results and Table 4

mechanism_certainty.comment: Design ceiling for an observational regression (JBI Cross-Sectional) is 2. Rated 1 (documented association) because the study establishes statistical associations between aggregate administrative/fiscal proxies (statutory local government category, per-capita NURM/UIDSSMT intergovernmental aid, and state fiscal decentralization index) and city-level tap-water coverage growth, while explicitly noting that local government capacity is measured via proxies and city-level institutional configurations are not directly observed (PDF p. 5, p. 12).
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 5, Variable measures; PDF pp. 10-12, Model results and Table 4

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines statutory local-government classification and jurisdictional mandates (municipal corporation vs. municipality vs. town panchayat), urban water infrastructure planning and city-size/category eligibility rules in national/state missions (NURM, UIDSSMT, AMRUT), multilevel federal-state-municipal governance and fiscal decentralization (institutional_fragmentation), and central-state-local intergovernmental grant transfers (political_coordination).
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 3-7, Literature review and Variable measures; PDF pp. 10-13, Model results and Conclusion

outcome_flags.comment: Primary outcome is city-level growth (2001-2011 percentage-point change) in public water supply service coverage, defined as the proportion of urban households whose primary drinking water source is municipal tap water accessed within the residence (household piped connection). Frequency/continuity and water quality are explicitly noted as unmeasured (PDF p. 12), and sanitation is not empirically modelled.
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF p. 2, Introduction; PDF p. 4, Footnote 4; PDF p. 5, Variable measures; PDF p. 6, Table 1

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Observational city-level regression with one observation per city (N = 3,547) modelling 2001-2011 change in census coverage against city- and state-level predictors measured across 2001-2011 (including 2011 Census administrative status, population, and density) without a quasi-experimental intervention/comparator design; appraised as an analytical observational cross-sectional/ecological regression.

sample_size.comment: Analytic sample in the descriptive tables and multilevel regressions is N = 3,547 statutory cities and towns enumerated in both the 2001 and 2011 Census of India across 21 states (note: categorical frequency counts in Tables 1 and 2—44 metropolitan cities, 43 medium cities, 380 small cities, and 3,091 small towns; 145 municipal corporations, 1,534 municipalities, and 1,879 town panchayats and others—sum to 3,558 before listwise/analytic restriction to N = 3,547).
sample_size.value: 3,547 urban local governments (statutory cities and towns) nested within 21 states
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 6, Table 1 footnotes b and f; PDF p. 10, Table 3; PDF p. 11, Table 4

study_design.comment: Models single-period decadal change (2001-2011 percentage-point change in city-level household tap-water coverage) across 3,547 cities nested in 21 states via maximum likelihood random-effects multilevel linear regression on city-level and state-level predictors measured in 2001, 2004, 2007, and 2011, without a quasi-experimental intervention comparator.
study_design.value: Observational ecological city-level study using two-level nested multilevel linear regression with state random effects (2001 and 2011 Census of India data)
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 4-8, Data and methodology
